chunks.topic_title: Critical Care of the High-Risk Surgical Patient
chunks.content: Critical Care of the High-Risk Surgical Patient. High-risk surgical patient for FRCA Final/FFICM: P-POSSUM/SORT/CPET/CFS, level-2/3 admission, structured handover, GDT, MINS surveillance, NELA/CPOC standards. Also known as: High-risk surgical patient, Perioperative critical care, P-POSSUM, SORT, CPET, MINS, NELA, CPOC. Keywords: high risk surgical patient, P-POSSUM, CPET, MINS surveillance, NELA.

chunks.topic_title: Critical Care of the High-Risk Surgical Patient
chunks.content:
Critical Care of the High-Risk Surgical Patient — Q: How are high-risk surgical patients identified preoperatively?
A: Combine clinical (frailty, METs <4, P-POSSUM), biochemical (NT-proBNP, troponin) and functional (CPET — anaerobic threshold <11 mL/kg/min, VO₂peak <15) measures; aggregate predicts 30-day mortality >5%.

chunks.topic_title: Critical Care of the High-Risk Surgical Patient
chunks.content:
Critical Care of the High-Risk Surgical Patient — Q: What is the evidence for goal-directed haemodynamic therapy?
A: Meta-analyses (OPTIMISE, Cochrane 2013) show GDT with SV optimisation reduces complications and length of stay in moderate–high-risk surgery but no consistent mortality benefit; effect is greatest where baseline care is poor.

chunks.topic_title: Critical Care of the High-Risk Surgical Patient
chunks.content:
Critical Care of the High-Risk Surgical Patient — Q: When should postoperative ICU admission be offered?
A: After major surgery in patients with predicted mortality >5%, intra-operative instability requiring vasopressors >2 h, massive transfusion, persistent lactate >2 mmol/L, or unplanned organ support — per RCoA/AAGBI peri-operative care guidelines.
Paediatric Intensive Care (Intensive Care · exams: fficm, edic). Age-specific physiology, paediatric sepsis, congenital heart disease, neurocritical care, sedation, and resuscitation

Paediatric Intensive Care. Paediatric intensive care for FFICM: age-specific physiology, paediatric sepsis, congenital heart disease, paediatric neurocritical care, sedation, resuscitation. Also known as: Paediatric ICU, PICU, Paediatric sepsis, Paediatric resuscitation, Paediatric critical care. Keywords: paediatric ICU, PICU, paediatric sepsis, paediatric resuscitation.

Paediatric Intensive Care — Q: What fluid resuscitation strategy is recommended for paediatric septic shock?
A: 10–20 mL/kg balanced crystalloid boluses with reassessment after each, up to 40–60 mL/kg in the first hour; start adrenaline or noradrenaline early if fluid-refractory rather than continuing boluses (FEAST, SSC paediatric 2020).

Paediatric Intensive Care — Q: What is paediatric ARDS (PARDS) and how does ventilation differ?
A: Berlin-equivalent criteria (PALICC 2015) using OI rather than P/F ratio; use Vt 5–8 mL/kg PBW, plateau ≤28 cmH₂O, permissive hypercapnia (pH ≥7.20), PEEP titrated 8–15, prone if OI ≥12.

Paediatric Intensive Care — Q: How is intraosseous access used in paediatric resuscitation?
A: Insert in the proximal tibia (or distal femur/humerus) if IV access fails within 60–90 s in shock or arrest; flow rates approach IV after a 10 mL saline flush, and all resus drugs can be given at standard doses.

Burns Intensive Care (Intensive Care · exams: final, fficm, edic). Major-burn pathophysiology, airway/inhalation injury, fluid resuscitation (Parkland/modified Brooke), escharotomy, sepsis, nutrition, AKI, and ICU referral criteria

Burns Intensive Care. Major burns critical care for FRCA/FFICM: pathophysiology, airway and inhalation injury, fluid resuscitation (Parkland/modified Brooke), escharotomy, AKI, sepsis. Also known as: Burns ICU, Major burn, Inhalation injury, Parkland formula, Modified Brooke, Escharotomy. Keywords: burns ICU, Parkland formula, inhalation injury, escharotomy.

Burns Intensive Care — Q: How is fluid resuscitation calculated for major burns?
A: Modified Parkland: 3–4 mL/kg/%TBSA Hartmann's in the first 24 h, half in the first 8 h from time of burn; titrate to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h (adults), 1 mL/kg/h (children) — avoid fluid creep.

Burns Intensive Care — Q: What are the indications for early intubation in inhalational injury?
A: Stridor, hoarseness, facial/oropharyngeal burns, soot in the airway, carbonaceous sputum, hypoxia, large body-surface burns (>30%) or anticipated transfer; the airway can swell rapidly after fluid resuscitation.

Burns Intensive Care — Q: How is carbon monoxide poisoning managed in burns?
A: 100% oxygen via non-rebreather or ETT (reduces CO half-life from 5 h to ~80 min); consider hyperbaric oxygen if COHb >25%, loss of consciousness, neurological signs, pregnancy or persistent acidosis.
Organ Donation (Intensive Care · exams: fficm, edic). Brainstem death testing, DCD, DBD, donor optimisation

Organ Donation. Organ donation for FFICM/EDIC: brainstem death testing, DBD vs DCD pathways, donor optimisation, family approach, legal and ethical framework. Also known as: Organ donation, Brainstem death, DBD, DCD, Donation after brain death, Donation after circulatory death, Donor optimisation. Keywords: organ donation, brainstem death, DBD DCD, donor optimisation.

Organ Donation — Q: What are the UK criteria for brainstem death testing?
A: Coma of known irreversible cause, exclusion of confounders (drugs, hypothermia <34 °C, metabolic/endocrine disturbance), absent brainstem reflexes (pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, oculovestibular, gag, cough) and apnoea test with PaCO₂ rise >0.5 kPa above 6.0 kPa with pH <7.40 (AoMRC 2008).

Organ Donation — Q: What physiological derangements occur after brainstem death?
A: Catecholamine storm followed by vasodilation, diabetes insipidus (DDAVP/vasopressin), hypothermia, coagulopathy and pituitary failure; manage with the 'rule of 100s' — SBP >100, urine output ~100 mL/h, PaO₂ >100, Hb >100 g/L.

Organ Donation — Q: How does DCD differ from DBD for donation?
A: DCD (Maastricht III) occurs after planned withdrawal with death by circulatory criteria and a 5-minute 'no-touch' period; warm ischaemic time limits organ viability (typically <30 min for liver, <2 h for kidney) and outcomes are slightly inferior for some grafts but improve donor numbers.
Prognostication, Ethics & Outcomes (Intensive Care · exams: final, fficm, edic). Prognostic scoring, treatment escalation plans, medical ethics, withdrawal of treatment, PICS, long-term outcomes

Prognostication, Ethics & Outcomes. Prognostication and ethics in ICU for FRCA Final/FFICM: prognostic scoring, treatment escalation plans, withdrawal of treatment, PICS and long-term outcomes. Also known as: ICU prognostication, Treatment escalation plan, Withdrawal of treatment, PICS, Post-intensive care syndrome, ICU ethics. Keywords: ICU prognostication, treatment escalation plan, PICS, withdrawal of treatment.

Prognostication, Ethics & Outcomes — Q: What ethical framework underpins withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment?
A: Four principles (Beauchamp & Childress): autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice — applied through best-interests assessment under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, involving family, IMCA if no representative, and shared decision-making.

Prognostication, Ethics & Outcomes — Q: What is the distinction between withholding and withdrawing treatment?
A: Ethically and legally equivalent in UK law — both are decisions not to provide treatment that is not in the patient's best interests; withdrawal is not euthanasia, as intent is to relieve suffering, not to cause death (GMC 2010, Aintree v James 2013).

Prognostication, Ethics & Outcomes — Q: How are prognostic scores used responsibly at end of life?
A: APACHE IV, SOFA and clinical frailty scales inform but never determine individual decisions; integrate with disease trajectory, response to treatment and patient values — never withdraw on score alone.

End-of-Life Care & Communication (Intensive Care · exams: fficm, edic). Breaking bad news, family meetings, withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment, symptom control at end of life, conflict resolution, cultural and spiritual care

End-of-Life Care & Communication. End-of-life care for FFICM: breaking bad news, family meetings, withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment, symptom control, conflict resolution, cultural care. Also known as: End of life care, Withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment, WLST, Breaking bad news, Family meetings ICU, Palliative care ICU. Keywords: end of life ICU, WLST, family meetings, breaking bad news.

End-of-Life Care & Communication — Q: What is the SPIKES framework for breaking bad news?
A: Setting up, Perception ('what do you understand?'), Invitation (how much do they want to know), Knowledge (information in chunks, warning shot), Empathy (acknowledge emotion), Strategy and Summary.

End-of-Life Care & Communication — Q: How should family meetings be structured in ICU?
A: Pre-meeting team huddle, named clinician leader, quiet private space, introductions, summary of clinical picture, exploration of patient values, shared decision-making, agreed plan and documentation; offer follow-up.

End-of-Life Care & Communication — Q: What is the role of advance care planning in ICU?
A: Advance decisions to refuse treatment (ADRT, valid and applicable under MCA 2005) and lasting power of attorney bind treatment decisions; ReSPECT forms guide but do not bind; always seek patient or representative input before withdrawal.

Non-Technical Skills & Human Factors (Intensive Care · exams: fficm, edic). ANTS framework, situation awareness, decision-making, teamwork, leadership, crisis resource management, debriefing, just culture

Non-Technical Skills & Human Factors. Non-technical skills and human factors for FRCA/FFICM: ANTS framework, situation awareness, decision-making, teamwork, leadership, CRM, debriefing, just culture. Also known as: Non-technical skills, Human factors, ANTS, Anaesthetists Non-Technical Skills, Crisis resource management, CRM, Debriefing. Keywords: ANTS, human factors, crisis resource management, non-technical skills FRCA.

Non-Technical Skills & Human Factors — Q: What are the four domains of ANTS (Anaesthetists' Non-Technical Skills)?
A: Task management, team working, situation awareness and decision making — each with behavioural markers used for structured debrief and assessment (Fletcher et al., BJA 2003).

Non-Technical Skills & Human Factors — Q: What is the difference between 'shared mental model' and 'situation awareness'?
A: Situation awareness is individual perception of cues, comprehension and projection (Endsley); shared mental model is the team-wide common understanding of the problem and plan — built by closed-loop communication and structured handover (e.g. SBAR).

Non-Technical Skills & Human Factors — Q: How does cognitive aid use improve crisis management?
A: Cognitive aids (e.g. AAGBI Quick Reference Handbook, ASA Critical Events) reduce omission errors in low-frequency emergencies — RCTs show measurable improvement when a dedicated reader is appointed within the team.
Preoperative Assessment (Perioperative Medicine · exams: final). Risk stratification, CPET, cardiac risk indices, optimisation

Preoperative Assessment. Preoperative assessment for FRCA/FFICM: ASA, RCRI, SORT, CPET thresholds, NICE NG45 investigations, medication management and PBM. Also known as: Preoperative assessment, Perioperative risk stratification, RCRI, SORT, CPET, NICE NG45, Patient blood management, Pre-op anaemia. Keywords: preoperative assessment FRCA, RCRI, CPET anaerobic threshold, NICE NG45, patient blood management, pre-op anaemia.

Preoperative Assessment — Q: What is the prognostic value of CPET anaerobic threshold (AT) before major surgery?
A: An AT <11 mL/kg/min predicts increased postoperative cardiopulmonary morbidity and 30/90-day mortality after major non-cardiac surgery; 11–14 mL/kg/min is intermediate risk and >14 mL/kg/min low risk (Older 1993; POM-HR).

Preoperative Assessment — Q: When should elective non-cardiac surgery be deferred after PCI?
A: At least 4 weeks after balloon angioplasty, 6 weeks (ideally 3 months) after a bare-metal stent, and 6 months (ideally 12 months) after a drug-eluting stent — to allow dual antiplatelet therapy without premature interruption (ACC/AHA 2024).

Preoperative Assessment — Q: How is the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (Lee) interpreted?
A: Six predictors (high-risk surgery, IHD, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, creatinine >177 µmol/L): 0 ≈ 0.4%, 1 ≈ 1%, 2 ≈ 2.4%, ≥3 ≈ 5.4% risk of a major cardiac event at 30 days.
Enhanced Recovery (ERAS) (Perioperative Medicine · exams: final). Perioperative care pathways, prehabilitation, goal-directed therapy

Enhanced Recovery (ERAS). Enhanced Recovery After Surgery for FRCA Final: ERAS principles, surgical stress response, prehabilitation, PONV prophylaxis, landmark trials and specialty protocols. Also known as: Enhanced recovery, ERAS, Fast track surgery, Perioperative care pathway, Prehabilitation, PONV prophylaxis. Keywords: ERAS FRCA, enhanced recovery surgery, ERAS principles, prehabilitation, PONV prophylaxis, LAFA trial, RELIEF trial.

Enhanced Recovery (ERAS) — Q: What are the core preoperative elements of an ERAS pathway?
A: Patient education, optimisation of comorbidities (anaemia, smoking, nutrition), avoidance of prolonged fasting with carbohydrate loading up to 2 hours before induction, and avoidance of routine mechanical bowel preparation in colorectal surgery.

Enhanced Recovery (ERAS) — Q: Why is goal-directed fluid therapy preferred over fixed-volume regimens in ERAS?
A: Stroke-volume optimisation with small balanced crystalloid boluses titrated to dynamic indices reduces postoperative complications and length of stay compared with both liberal and overly restrictive fixed regimens (POM-O, OPTIMISE).

Enhanced Recovery (ERAS) — Q: How does opioid-sparing analgesia fit into ERAS?
A: A multimodal regimen — paracetamol, NSAIDs (where safe), regional or neuraxial blocks, dexamethasone and adjuncts such as lidocaine or ketamine — reduces opioid requirements, postoperative ileus and PONV, supporting earlier mobilisation and oral intake.
Perioperative Fluid Therapy (Perioperative Medicine · exams: final, fficm). Crystalloids vs colloids, goal-directed, fluid responsiveness

Perioperative Fluid Therapy. Perioperative fluid therapy for FRCA/FFICM: crystalloids vs colloids, goal-directed fluid therapy, revised Starling equation, glycocalyx, and landmark trials (SMART, RELIEF, BaSICS). Also known as: Perioperative fluid therapy, GDFT, Goal-directed fluid therapy, Crystalloids vs colloids, Fluid responsiveness, Glycocalyx, Revised Starling equation. Keywords: perioperative fluid therapy FRCA, GDFT, goal-directed fluid therapy, crystalloids vs colloids, SMART trial, RELIEF trial, glycocalyx, fluid responsiveness.

Perioperative Fluid Therapy — Q: Why are balanced crystalloids preferred over 0.9% saline for perioperative resuscitation?
A: Large volumes of 0.9% saline cause hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis and are associated with increased acute kidney injury and adverse renal events (SMART, SALT-ED). Balanced crystalloids (Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte) have a more physiological chloride content.

Perioperative Fluid Therapy — Q: How is fluid responsiveness assessed in a mechanically ventilated patient?
A: With dynamic indices such as stroke volume variation or pulse pressure variation >12–13%, in sinus rhythm with tidal volume ≥8 mL/kg; if these conditions are not met, use a passive leg-raise manoeuvre or a 250 mL fluid challenge with stroke-volume reassessment.

Perioperative Fluid Therapy — Q: When are starch-based colloids contraindicated?
A: Hydroxyethyl starches should be avoided in sepsis and critical illness (CHEST, 6S — increased AKI and mortality) and are not licensed for ICU use in the UK or EU.
Vascular Access Devices (Perioperative Medicine · exams: primary, final, fficm). Cannulae, midlines, PICCs, CVCs, vascaths, trauma lines (RIC/MAC) and Swan-Ganz introducer sheaths

Vascular Access Devices. Vascular access devices for FRCA Primary/Final/FFICM: peripheral cannulae, midlines, PICCs, CVCs, vascaths, trauma lines (RIC/MAC), Swan-Ganz introducers, and long-term tunnelled devices. Also known as: Vascular access devices, Central venous catheter, CVC, PICC, Peripheral cannula, Midline catheter, Vascath, Trauma line, RIC, MAC, Swan-Ganz sheath, Portacath, Hickman line. Keywords: vascular access devices FRCA, CVC anaesthesia, PICC line, peripheral cannula, midline catheter, vascath, trauma line RIC MAC, Swan-Ganz sheath, Portacath, Hickman line.

Vascular Access Devices — Q: How is the maximum safe infusion rate for a peripheral cannula determined?
A: By Hagen–Poiseuille — flow is proportional to the fourth power of internal radius and inversely proportional to length. A short, wide-bore (16G or 14G) cannula delivers far greater flow than a longer central catheter of equivalent gauge.

Vascular Access Devices — Q: When is a midline preferred over a PICC?
A: For peripherally compatible therapies of 1–4 weeks duration (e.g. antibiotics, fluids, non-irritant chemotherapy). Vesicants, parenteral nutrition or hyperosmolar/extreme-pH drugs require a central-tip device such as a PICC or CVC.

Vascular Access Devices — Q: What are the key complications of internal jugular CVC insertion?
A: Carotid puncture, pneumothorax (lower than subclavian but not zero), arrhythmias from wire or catheter contact, air embolism, catheter-related bloodstream infection, and late venous stenosis or thrombosis. Ultrasound guidance is mandatory (NICE TA49).
Cardiovascular Co-Existing Disease (Perioperative Medicine · exams: primary, final, fficm). IHD, valvular disease, heart failure, arrhythmias, pacemakers/ICDs, pulmonary hypertension, ACHD

Cardiovascular Co-Existing Disease. Perioperative cardiovascular disease for FRCA Final: IHD, valvular lesions, heart failure, arrhythmias, devices, pulmonary hypertension and ACHD. Also known as: Cardiovascular disease, Ischaemic heart disease, Valvular heart disease, Aortic stenosis, Heart failure, Pulmonary hypertension, Adult congenital heart disease, ACHD. Keywords: cardiovascular disease FRCA, perioperative cardiac risk, aortic stenosis anaesthesia, pulmonary hypertension, heart failure surgery.

Cardiovascular Co-Existing Disease — Q: What are the haemodynamic goals for severe aortic stenosis?
A: Maintain sinus rhythm, a normal or slightly low heart rate (60–80), adequate preload and high systemic vascular resistance — use phenylephrine or vasopressin first-line for hypotension, and avoid agents that drop SVR or cause tachycardia.

Cardiovascular Co-Existing Disease — Q: How should a pacemaker-dependent patient be managed when monopolar diathermy is required?
A: Reprogramme to an asynchronous mode (DOO/VOO) or apply a clinical magnet, position the diathermy return plate so the current path does not cross the device, use short bipolar bursts where possible, and check the device postoperatively.

Cardiovascular Co-Existing Disease — Q: What are the anaesthetic principles in pulmonary hypertension?
A: Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia and high airway pressures — all increase pulmonary vascular resistance. Maintain RV preload and coronary perfusion pressure, use noradrenaline or vasopressin for systemic hypotension, and have inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (NO, iloprost) available.

Cardiovascular Co-Existing Disease — Q: At what blood pressure should an elective case be cancelled for hypertension?
A: Per the AAGBI/BHS 2016 joint guideline, proceed if pre-assessment BP is <180 mmHg systolic AND <110 mmHg diastolic. Above this, refer back to primary care for optimisation rather than treating acutely on the day — there is no evidence that short-term in-hospital lowering reduces perioperative cardiac risk and rapid drops may cause harm.

Cardiovascular Co-Existing Disease — Q: How should ACE inhibitors and ARBs be managed on the day of surgery?
A: Both ESC/ESA 2022 and the 2024 ACC/AHA perioperative guideline recommend withholding ACE-I/ARB on the morning of surgery when they are prescribed for hypertension, to reduce intra-operative hypotension. POISE-3 (2023) supports this 'hypotension-avoidance' approach with a MAP target ≥80 mmHg. Restart within 48 h once the patient is euvolaemic with stable renal function.

Cardiovascular Co-Existing Disease — Q: How do you manage true hypertensive emergency before urgent surgery?
A: Use an arterial line and titrate IV antihypertensives (labetalol or esmolol for dissection/phaeochromocytoma surge, GTN for ACS/pulmonary oedema, magnesium + labetalol for eclampsia) to lower MAP by no more than 20–25% in the first hour, then to around 160/100 mmHg over 2–6 h. Treat reversible precipitants (pain, hypoxia, hypercarbia, raised ICP) first. Truly time-critical surgery should not be delayed for chronic hypertension alone.
Respiratory Co-Existing Disease (Perioperative Medicine · exams: primary, final, fficm). Asthma, COPD, OSA, restrictive lung disease, pulmonary fibrosis, respiratory infections

Respiratory Co-Existing Disease. Perioperative respiratory disease for FRCA Final: asthma, COPD, OSA, restrictive lung disease, pulmonary fibrosis and respiratory infections. Also known as: Respiratory disease, Asthma anaesthesia, COPD surgery, Obstructive sleep apnoea, OSA, Pulmonary fibrosis, Restrictive lung disease. Keywords: respiratory disease FRCA, asthma anaesthesia, COPD perioperative, OSA surgery, pulmonary fibrosis.

Respiratory Co-Existing Disease — Q: How should the asthmatic patient be optimised before elective anaesthesia?
A: Continue inhalers including on the day of surgery, ensure no recent exacerbation or URTI (defer 2–6 weeks if present), give nebulised salbutamol pre-induction if reactive, and prefer sevoflurane (bronchodilator) over desflurane (airway irritant).

Respiratory Co-Existing Disease — Q: What ventilation strategy minimises COPD-related complications intraoperatively?
A: Lung-protective ventilation with tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg IBW, a prolonged expiratory time (low I:E ratio), permissive hypercapnia and judicious PEEP — to avoid dynamic hyperinflation and auto-PEEP.

Respiratory Co-Existing Disease — Q: Why is OSA important in postoperative planning?
A: STOP-BANG ≥5 indicates high risk of perioperative respiratory adverse events. Patients need opioid-sparing analgesia, CPAP available in recovery and on the ward, and extended monitoring; long-acting opioids and benzodiazepines should be avoided.
Endocrine Co-Existing Disease (Perioperative Medicine · exams: primary, final, fficm). Diabetes mellitus, thyroid disease, adrenal disorders, phaeochromocytoma, carcinoid syndrome

Endocrine Co-Existing Disease. Perioperative endocrine disease for FRCA Final: diabetes mellitus, thyroid disorders, adrenal insufficiency, phaeochromocytoma and carcinoid syndrome. Also known as: Endocrine disease, Diabetes mellitus surgery, Thyroid storm, Phaeochromocytoma anaesthesia, Adrenal insufficiency, Carcinoid syndrome, Steroid supplementation. Keywords: endocrine disease FRCA, diabetes perioperative, phaeochromocytoma anaesthesia, thyroid storm, steroid cover surgery, carcinoid syndrome.

Endocrine Co-Existing Disease — Q: What perioperative glucose target and insulin strategy apply in diabetes?
A: Aim for capillary blood glucose 6–10 mmol/L (acceptable 4–12). Continue 80% of usual long-acting basal insulin; use a variable-rate insulin infusion (VRIII) for prolonged starvation, complex surgery or poor glycaemic control (CPOC/JBDS 2023).

Endocrine Co-Existing Disease — Q: How is phaeochromocytoma prepared for surgery?
A: α-blockade first (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin titrated over 10–14 days) until orthostatic hypotension is achieved, followed by β-blockade only once α-blockade is established — never β-block first, as unopposed α-activity precipitates hypertensive crisis.

Endocrine Co-Existing Disease — Q: How are major-surgery steroid requirements managed in chronic steroid users?
A: Continue the usual dose plus IV hydrocortisone — typically 25 mg at induction for minor, 50 mg + 25 mg 8-hourly for moderate, and 100 mg + 50 mg 8-hourly for major surgery — to prevent Addisonian crisis from HPA-axis suppression.
Neurological Co-Existing Disease (Perioperative Medicine · exams: primary, final, fficm). Myasthenia gravis, epilepsy, MS, Parkinson's, MND, muscular dystrophies, spinal cord injury

Neurological Co-Existing Disease. Perioperative neurological disease for FRCA Final: myasthenia gravis, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's, motor neuron disease, muscular dystrophies and spinal cord injury. Also known as: Neurological disease, Myasthenia gravis anaesthesia, Epilepsy surgery, Multiple sclerosis anaesthesia, Parkinson's disease surgery, Motor neuron disease, Muscular dystrophy anaesthesia, Spinal cord injury anaesthesia. Keywords: neurological disease FRCA, myasthenia gravis anaesthesia, epilepsy perioperative, Parkinson's anaesthesia, spinal cord injury anaesthesia.

Neurological Co-Existing Disease — Q: How do myasthenia gravis patients respond to neuromuscular blocking drugs?
A: They are markedly sensitive to non-depolarising NMBs (use 10–20% of normal dose, ideally rocuronium with sugammadex reversal) and relatively resistant to suxamethonium. Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring is essential.

Neurological Co-Existing Disease — Q: What are the anaesthetic implications of Parkinson's disease?
A: Never omit l-dopa (risk of neuroleptic malignant–like syndrome and rigidity); avoid D2-antagonists (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, droperidol, haloperidol); and anticipate autonomic instability, aspiration risk and postoperative confusion.

Neurological Co-Existing Disease — Q: Why is suxamethonium dangerous more than 24 hours after spinal cord injury?
A: Upregulation of extra-junctional acetylcholine receptors causes massive potassium efflux on depolarisation, producing life-threatening hyperkalaemia and cardiac arrest. Use a non-depolarising NMB instead.

Haematological Co-Existing Disease (Perioperative Medicine · exams: primary, final, fficm). Perioperative anaemia (incl. iron deficiency), thrombocytopenia and neutropenia — patient blood management, transfusion thresholds and procedural safety

Haematological Co-Existing Disease — Q: When should preoperative anaemia screening be performed?
A: CPOC (2023) and NATA (2017) recommend identifying anaemia at the point of listing for major elective surgery, allowing at least 6 weeks for investigation and treatment. A full blood count, ferritin, transferrin saturation, B12, folate and renal function form the minimum panel; CRP is needed to interpret ferritin in inflammation (functional iron deficiency).

Haematological Co-Existing Disease — Q: What is the safe platelet count for spinal or epidural anaesthesia?
A: AAGBI (2013) and BSH (2017) support neuraxial blockade with a platelet count ≥80 ×10⁹/L provided the count is stable and the cause of thrombocytopenia is benign. Counts of 50–80 ×10⁹/L require an explicit risk–benefit assessment; below 50 ×10⁹/L neuraxial techniques are generally avoided. Never transfuse platelets in HIT, TTP or ITP without specialist advice.

Haematological Co-Existing Disease — Q: How do you manage a patient presenting for emergency surgery with severe thrombocytopenia of unknown cause?
A: Discuss with haematology before transfusing. Avoid platelets in TTP/HIT (may worsen thrombosis). For life-threatening bleeding, give platelets to a target of >50 ×10⁹/L (>100 for CNS/eye), correct fibrinogen (>1.5 g/L), and consider TXA 1 g. Use general rather than neuraxial anaesthesia and minimise invasive lines where possible.

Haematological Co-Existing Disease — Q: What antibiotic should be given for suspected neutropenic sepsis?
A: Per NICE neutropenic-sepsis guidance, empirical piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV (or meropenem if previous resistance / β-lactam allergy with cross-reactivity assessment) within 1 hour of recognition, after blood cultures. Add vancomycin or teicoplanin only for suspected line infection, MRSA risk or severe mucositis.

Hepatic Co-Existing Disease (Perioperative Medicine · exams: final, fficm). Cirrhosis, portal hypertension, Child-Pugh & MELD risk, altered pharmacology, coagulation, hepatorenal syndrome, anaesthesia for non-hepatic surgery in liver disease

Hepatic Co-Existing Disease. Perioperative hepatic disease for FRCA Final: Child-Pugh and MELD risk, cirrhosis physiology, rebalanced coagulation, drug choices and hepatorenal syndrome. Also known as: Hepatic disease, Cirrhosis anaesthesia, Child-Pugh score, MELD score, Hepatorenal syndrome, Hepatopulmonary syndrome, Portopulmonary hypertension. Keywords: hepatic disease FRCA, cirrhosis anaesthesia, MELD perioperative, hepatorenal syndrome, rebalanced haemostasis, VOCAL-Penn.

Hepatic Co-Existing Disease — Q: How is preoperative risk stratified in cirrhosis for non-hepatic surgery?
A: Combine Child-Pugh class (A/B/C) and MELD score — MELD <10 is low risk, 10–15 intermediate, and >15 high (>20 prohibitive for elective surgery). The VOCAL-Penn score outperforms MELD for surgical mortality prediction.

Hepatic Co-Existing Disease — Q: Why should FFP not be used to 'correct' the INR in stable cirrhosis?
A: Cirrhotic coagulopathy is a rebalanced state — both pro- and anti-coagulant factors are reduced. FFP raises portal pressure (worsening variceal bleeding risk) and adds volume without correcting the underlying defect; thromboelastography (ROTEM/TEG) guides targeted therapy.

Hepatic Co-Existing Disease — Q: How is hepatorenal syndrome managed perioperatively?
A: Splanchnic vasoconstrictor (terlipressin or noradrenaline) plus 20% human albumin (1 g/kg on day 1, then 20–40 g/day). Diuretics, large-volume crystalloid and low-dose dopamine all worsen outcome; definitive treatment is liver transplantation.
Genetic Syndromes & Anaesthesia (Perioperative Medicine · exams: final, fficm). MH, dystrophinopathies, myotonic dystrophy, BChE deficiency, Down, Marfan, sickle cell, porphyria

Genetic Syndromes & Anaesthesia. Perioperative genetic syndromes for FRCA Final: malignant hyperthermia, muscular dystrophies, Down syndrome, Marfan, achondroplasia, sickle cell, porphyria and BChE deficiency. Also known as: Genetic syndromes, Malignant hyperthermia, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Down syndrome anaesthesia, Marfan syndrome anaesthesia, Achondroplasia anaesthesia, Sickle cell anaesthesia, Porphyria anaesthesia, Pseudocholinesterase deficiency. Keywords: genetic syndromes FRCA, malignant hyperthermia anaesthesia, DMD anaesthesia, Down syndrome anaesthesia, Marfan syndrome anaesthesia, sickle cell surgery, acute intermittent porphyria.

Genetic Syndromes & Anaesthesia — Q: How is malignant hyperthermia treated?
A: Stop all volatile agents and suxamethonium, switch to TIVA, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen via a clean circuit, give IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg repeated up to 10 mg/kg (more if required), cool actively, and treat hyperkalaemia, acidosis and arrhythmias (AAGBI 2020).

Genetic Syndromes & Anaesthesia — Q: Why is suxamethonium contraindicated in Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy?
A: Even sub-clinical dystrophinopathy can precipitate rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest after suxamethonium or prolonged volatile exposure — TIVA with non-depolarising NMBs is mandatory.

Genetic Syndromes & Anaesthesia — Q: What are the airway considerations in Down syndrome?
A: Macroglossia, narrow nasopharynx, subglottic stenosis (use a smaller ETT than predicted) and atlanto-axial instability (careful neck positioning, neutral head) — plus a high prevalence of congenital cardiac disease and obstructive sleep apnoea.
Atomic Structure & Chemical Bonding (Chemistry Foundations · exams: primary). Electron configuration, ionic/covalent/metallic bonds, intermolecular forces, electronegativity

Atomic Structure & Chemical Bonding — Q: Why does desflurane boil at room temperature while halothane boils at 50 °C?
A: Halothane carries heavy bromine and chlorine atoms whose large, polarisable electron clouds generate strong van der Waals forces, holding molecules together until ~50 °C. Desflurane has only small fluorine atoms with weak van der Waals attraction, so it boils at 23.5 °C — requiring the heated, pressurised Tec 6 vaporiser to deliver predictable partial pressures clinically.

Atomic Structure & Chemical Bonding — Q: Why is sodium chloride soluble in water but not in lipid?
A: NaCl is held in a high-energy ionic lattice (~787 kJ/mol). Water's strong O-H dipoles form hydration shells around Na⁺ and Cl⁻ that almost match the lattice energy, so the salt dissolves. Non-polar lipid solvents can only manage weak van der Waals interactions and cannot pay the lattice cost — which is why all electrolyte-containing IV fluids must be aqueous.

Atomic Structure & Chemical Bonding — Q: What determines whether a bond is ionic or covalent?
A: The electronegativity difference (ΔEN) between the atoms. ΔEN > ~1.7 (e.g. Na-Cl, 2.1) gives ionic bonding with full electron transfer. ΔEN < ~1.7 (e.g. C-H, 0.4) gives covalent bonding with electron sharing — polar covalent if ΔEN is 0.4–1.7 (e.g. O-H), non-polar if essentially zero (e.g. C-C). This in turn dictates solubility, melting point, and how drugs interact with receptors.
Acids, Bases & Buffer Systems (Chemistry Foundations · exams: primary, final, fficm). pH, pKa, Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, physiological buffers, strong vs weak acids

Acids, Bases & Buffer Systems — Q: What defines a buffer's effective range?
A: A buffer works best within ±1 pH unit of its pKa, where the Henderson–Hasselbalch ratio of weak acid to conjugate base lies between 10:1 and 1:10. The bicarbonate system (pKa 6.1) effectively buffers blood at pH 7.4 only because it is open — CO₂ is continuously removed by ventilation, regenerating capacity and uncoupling it from the closed-system pKa limit.

Acids, Bases & Buffer Systems — Q: How is base excess calculated and what does it mean?
A: Base excess is the amount of strong acid or base required to titrate 1 L of blood back to pH 7.40 at PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa, 37 °C and full oxygenation. Values outside ±2 mmol/L indicate a metabolic disturbance — positive in metabolic alkalosis or compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis, negative in metabolic acidosis or compensation for chronic respiratory alkalosis.

Acids, Bases & Buffer Systems — Q: Why does CO₂ acidify blood despite not being an acid?
A: CO₂ reacts with water (carbonic anhydrase in red cells) to form H₂CO₃, which dissociates to H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. A rise in PaCO₂ pushes the equilibrium right, generating H⁺ and lowering pH — the basis of respiratory acidosis. Hyperventilation does the reverse and rapidly raises pH.
Organic Chemistry for Anaesthetists (Chemistry Foundations · exams: primary). Functional groups, isomerism, chirality, and their relevance to drug structure and action

Organic Chemistry for Anaesthetists — Q: Why do ester local anaesthetics act for a shorter duration than amides?
A: Esters (procaine, amethocaine) are hydrolysed rapidly by plasma cholinesterase, giving half-lives of 1–10 min. Amides (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine) are metabolised slowly by hepatic CYP enzymes with half-lives of 1.5–3.5 h. Ester hydrolysis also liberates PABA, which explains the allergy risk that amides lack.

Organic Chemistry for Anaesthetists — Q: What is a chiral centre and why is ropivacaine an example?
A: A chiral centre is a carbon bonded to four different groups, generating two non-superimposable mirror-image enantiomers. Ropivacaine is the pure S(-)-enantiomer of its racemate; the R(+) form is more cardiotoxic. Single-enantiomer formulation gives ropivacaine a safer cardiovascular profile than racemic bupivacaine at equipotent doses.

Organic Chemistry for Anaesthetists — Q: How does pKa influence local anaesthetic onset?
A: At tissue pH 7.4, Henderson–Hasselbalch dictates the proportion of un-ionised (lipid-soluble) drug. Lidocaine (pKa 7.9) has more un-ionised drug at injection and crosses the nerve membrane in 2–5 min. Higher-pKa drugs (bupivacaine 8.1, procaine 8.9) are more ionised and slower to act.
Solutions & Concentration (Chemistry Foundations · exams: primary, final). Molarity, molality, osmolality, osmolarity, tonicity, colligative properties

Solutions & Concentration — Q: What is the difference between osmolarity and osmolality?
A: Osmolarity is osmoles per litre of solution (mOsm/L); osmolality is osmoles per kilogram of solvent (mOsm/kg). Plasma values overlap at 285–295, but osmolality is preferred clinically because it is independent of temperature and unaffected by the volume occupied by plasma proteins and lipids.

Solutions & Concentration — Q: Why does 0.9% saline carry a risk of hyperchloraemic acidosis?
A: It contains 154 mmol/L Cl⁻ — well above the plasma range of 95–105. Large volumes raise plasma Cl⁻, lowering the strong-ion difference and producing a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Balanced crystalloids (Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte) substitute lactate, acetate or gluconate for some Cl⁻ to avoid this.

Solutions & Concentration — Q: How do you convert percentage concentration to mg/mL?
A: A 1% solution = 1 g/100 mL = 10 mg/mL. So 2% lidocaine is 20 mg/mL, 0.5% bupivacaine is 5 mg/mL, and 1:200 000 adrenaline (1 g per 200 000 mL) is 5 µg/mL. This conversion is essential when calculating maximum safe local anaesthetic doses from the syringe label.
Oxidation, Reduction & Electrochemistry (Chemistry Foundations · exams: primary). Redox reactions, electrode potentials, clinical electrodes, free radicals

Oxidation, Reduction & Electrochemistry — Q: Why is methaemoglobin clinically dangerous?
A: In methaemoglobin the haem iron is oxidised from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ and cannot bind oxygen, while remaining haems bind O₂ more tightly (left-shifted curve) — so tissue delivery falls. Levels >15% cause cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen; >50% cause coma; >70% are fatal. Treat with IV methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg, which regenerates Fe²⁺ via NADPH-methaemoglobin reductase.

Oxidation, Reduction & Electrochemistry — Q: How does a fuel cell oxygen analyser work?
A: A galvanic (fuel) cell consumes O₂ at a lead anode (Pb → Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻), generating a current proportional to O₂ partial pressure at the gold cathode (O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻). It is self-powered, accurate to ±3%, and lasts ~12 months because the anode is consumed.

Oxidation, Reduction & Electrochemistry — Q: Which inhaled anaesthetics are degraded by CO₂ absorbents?
A: Sevoflurane reacts with strong bases (KOH, NaOH) in soda-lime to form Compound A, a vinyl ether with renal toxicity in rats. Desflurane, isoflurane and enflurane react with dry CO₂ absorbent to generate carbon monoxide. Both risks are mitigated by using KOH/NaOH-free absorbents (e.g. Amsorb Plus) and avoiding desiccated absorbent.
